problem: No existing VLN benchmark or method targets agricultural scenes. Prior benchmarks cover residences (R2R, REVERIE, VLN-CE), streets (Touchdown) or aerial views (AerialVLN). They mostly use high-mounted, panoramic or synthetic cameras that do not match small agricultural robots with one low front-facing RGB camera. Prompted VLM navigators also lose track of which part of a long, noisy instruction they are executing.
motivation: Most agricultural robots (phenotyping, spraying, harvesting) still move by manual teleoperation or fixed rails, which limits mobility. Language-guided navigation could make them autonomous. A prompted GPT-4.1 mini agent handled short instructions well but collapsed on long ones: SR dropped from 0.51 at 2 subtasks to 0.14 at 3 or more. The authors attribute this to failure to track instruction progress, and draw on the human 'to-do list' habit as a remedy.
key_idea: Decompose the instruction once into a structured Subtask List with start/end conditions and pending/doing/done states, then let a lightweight VLM choose low-level actions from the current front-camera frame while attending only to the single active subtask.
insight: Explicit progress tracking over decomposed subtasks mainly pays off as instruction complexity grows. In Table 4 (GPT-4.1 mini), removing STL moves SR from 0.58 to 0.51 at 2 subtasks, 0.38 to 0.15 at 3, and 0.14 to 0.00 at 4 or more. However, STL consistently worsens NE (overall 2.91 vs 2.76; at 2 subtasks 2.32 vs 0.60), which the authors attribute to a conservative agent that stops too early. The gain also depends on the backbone: STL helps GPT-4.1 mini (+0.14 SR) and Gemini-1.5 flash (+0.04) but hurts Llama-4 maverick (0.33 vs 0.38), so the paper's 'excellent compatibility' claim is only partly supported. LLM-based decomposition (DILLM-VLN, AgriVLN) degrades more gracefully on long instructions than rule-based SIA-VLN (0.08 SR at ≥3 subtasks). Performance also varies strongly by scene (SR 0.66 farm vs 0.33 forest), even though instruction lengths are similar across scenes.
method: A2A benchmark: 1,560 expert-teleoperated episodes across 6 scene types (farm 372, greenhouse 258, forest 384, mountain 198, garden 258, village 90). Video comes from the front RGB camera of a Unitree Go2 Air quadruped at 0.38 m (1280x720, ~14 FPS). Instructions are deliberately casual and noisy: 10-99 words, avg 45.5; 2-8 subtasks, avg 2.6. Evaluation only.

Annotation: experts label the ground-truth action at every time step; consecutive identical actions are merged into JSON temporal intervals {action, time range}. Evaluation uses a custom 'simulator paradigm' built on these real videos (described only in the appendix).

Subtask List (STL) module: GPT-4.1 mini is prompted once per episode to turn instruction W into STL=<s_1..s_N>. Each s_i = {ID, description, start condition SC, end condition EC, state σ}. The prompt enforces three principles: Particle (subtasks are atomic), Synonymity (union of subtask meanings equals the instruction) and Connection (SC_i ≃ EC_{i-1}).

Decision making: at each step, GPT-4.1 mini receives the current front RGB frame I_t, the STL (not the raw instruction) and a crafted prompt P_DM. It outputs a low-level action from {FORWARD, LEFT ROTATE, RIGHT ROTATE, STOP}, a subtask state transition Δσ_t, and a reasoning trace ρ_t.

Subtask state machine: all subtasks start as pending. pending→doing is allowed only when the previous subtask is done; doing→done happens when the VLM judges completion. The VLM focuses on the 'doing' subtask, or else the first pending one, so attention stays on a single subtask.
Metrics: SR and NE (standard), plus ISR from LH-VLN, reported as mean successful subtasks / mean total subtasks per episode.

setting.backbone: GPT-4.1 mini (frozen, via API) for both instruction decomposition and per-step decision making; ablations swap in Gemini-1.5 flash and Llama-4 maverick
setting.observation: single front-facing monocular RGB frame (1280x720 video, ~14 FPS) from a quadruped at 0.38 m height
setting.action_space: discrete low-level {FORWARD, LEFT ROTATE, RIGHT ROTATE, STOP} (step/turn magnitudes not specified in main text)
setting.simulator: custom replay 'simulator paradigm' over pre-recorded real-world robot videos (A2A); details in appendix
setting.privileged: none stated. Note: observations come from pre-recorded expert-trajectory videos, so the agent does not control what it sees in the usual closed-loop sense (replay mechanism only described in the appendix).

numbers_note: A2A has no official train/val/test split: all 1,560 episodes are evaluation-only, recorded here as split 'test'. SR is printed as fractions (0.47) and converted to 0-100. The paper is internally inconsistent: the abstract and conclusion say STL improves SR 'from 0.31 to 0.42', the introduction says 'from 0.305 to 0.417', but Tables 2/3 report 0.33 → 0.47. Table values are used here. Average instruction length is given variously as 45.5, 41.2 and 46, and camera height as 0.38 m and 0.4 m. The success distance threshold and the NE computation over replayed video are not specified in the main text (appendix trimmed/unavailable). Per-scene results (Table 5, e.g. Farm SR 0.66 / NE 1.79, Forest SR 0.33 / NE 3.68) and the w/o-STL breakdown by subtask count (Table 4: SR 0.51/0.15/0.00 at 2/3/≥4 subtasks) are not listed as separate entries.
results: On the full A2A benchmark, AgriVLN (GPT-4.1 mini + STL) reaches SR 0.47 / NE 2.91. It beats the prompted GPT-4.1 mini baseline (SR 0.33 / NE 2.76), DILLM-VLN reproduced with GLM-4-32B (0.36 / 2.60) and SIA-VLN (0.31 / 3.24) on SR, though DILLM-VLN and the plain baseline have better NE. The gain is concentrated on long instructions: SR 0.35 vs 0.14 for the baseline at ≥3 subtasks, and 0.14 vs 0.00 at ≥4. Humans reach SR 0.87 / NE 0.57, leaving a large gap; random scores SR 0.09.
limitations: Evaluation is offline, on pre-recorded expert videos with a custom replay 'simulator' that is not described in the main text. There is no closed-loop real-robot deployment, and the benchmark is small (1,560 episodes, evaluation-only, 6 scenes).

STL raises SR but worsens NE (the agent stops too early), and it hurts SR for Llama-4 maverick. The authors report two failure modes: misunderstanding ambiguous instructions and inaccurate recognition of spatial distance.

Headline numbers are inconsistent across abstract, intro and tables (0.31→0.42 vs 0.305→0.417 vs 0.33→0.47). The 'comprehensively surpasses' claim does not hold for NE, and success criteria and ISR (reported as a count pair with method-dependent denominators) are only loosely defined.
